At the height of Trump's trade war with China, there were tariff hikes almost every week, and companies like Logitech responded by sharply raising prices on their products in the United States.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that these tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. Yet to date, no company has been seen passing the refunds on to consumers, and class-action lawsuits have been filed demanding that this be corrected…

The Trump Tariff Saga

Trump seized on the U.S. trade deficit with China last year, apparently fantasising that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the United States.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The U.S. lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour to support large brands producing consumer electronics at that scale.

Trump kept insisting that China paid the tariffs, but the reality was that American brands footed the bill when importing finished goods from China and then passed the cost on to consumers through higher prices. The tariff rate hit a peak of 145% during the height of the drama.

Take Logitech, for example — the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and ordered that the money already paid by U.S. businesses must be refunded. The refund process is currently under way.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, but none of the affected companies have yet announced plans to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds for consumers who paid the inflated prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's view

The principle here is indisputable: the companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to their customers, and are now getting the money back from the government. Morally, they ought to hand that money back to the consumers who bought their products during this period.

In practice, though, it is likely to be enormously challenging. Logitech would have to identify every transaction made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track what consumers actually paid, and work out what proportion of that was attributable to the tariffs.

Even if the lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set quite an interesting precedent — though it has to be said that class actions tend to benefit lawyers more than anyone else, with ordinary consumers typically receiving only a pittance.
